Foreword
Digital transformation is accelerating across the Middle East, North Africa, 
Afghanistan, and Pakistan (MENAAP) Region, reshaping economies, service 
delivery, and national development priorities. At the same time, conflict, fragility, 
and global disruptions are putting further pressure on growth. These pressures 
add to long-standing challenges, including limited job creation, unequal access

and global disruptions are putting further pressure on growth. These pressures 
add to long-standing challenges, including limited job creation, unequal access 
to services and opportunities, and uneven institutional capacity. As countries 
diversify their economies and prepare for a future shaped by artificial intelligence 
(AI), the central challenge is to ensure that digital transformation helps close 
these gaps rather than deepen them.
Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) can help address these challenges. DPI 
brings together shared digital building blocks—such as digital identity (digital 
ID), electronic signatures, payments, and data sharing—that governments and 
businesses can use to deliver many different services. When these building blocks 
work together, they can make services faster and less costly, expand access to 
underserved communities, and help countries respond more effectively in times 
of crisis.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, countries with DPI reached more than three 
times as many social benefit recipients as countries without it. But technology 
alone is not enough. Without strong institutions, adequate safeguards, and 
broad adoption, digital systems can remain fragmented, under-utilized, exclude 
the people they are meant to serve, expose personal data, and erode trust. 
Capturing the benefits while managing the risks starts with a clear picture of 
where the region stands.
To support these efforts, this report presents the first region-wide diagnostic 
of DPI in MENAAP countries, identifies barriers holding back DPI development 
and adoption, highlights opportunities for investment and reform across very 
different country contexts—from high-income economies to fragile and conflict-

The MENAAP region does not lack digital initiatives, but it needs to turn existing 
systems into connected, trusted, and widely used infrastructure. Seventeen 
countries have launched unified government service portals, yet only five have 
the back-end integration needed to make them genuine one-stop services. 
Where systems do not connect, governments rebuild the same capabilities 
repeatedly, services remain siloed, and crises expose the cost of fragmentation. IX

About the DPI and Services TF
The DPI and Services TF aims to increase the adoption and productive use of 
safe, inclusive, and interoperable digital building blocks and digitally enabled 
services. Operating as a One World Bank effort, it mobilizes expertise across 
digital transformation, social protection, health, financial inclusion, agriculture, 
governance, and education, among others. It also collaborates closely with 
Project FASTT on fast payment systems.

• Knowledge: generating evidence and translating standards into practical
tools.
• Action: supporting country-level DPI strategies, safe and inclusive building
blocks, and sectoral digital transformation.

he Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan (MENAAP) 
region sits at a turning point in its digital journey. Internet and mobile 
connectivity have expanded rapidly in the region, yet the productive 
use of digital tools for economic transactions remains among the 
lowest in the world. In 2024, only 44 percent of adults in the Middle East and 
North Africa (MENA) region made or received a digital payment, an indicator 
of the extent to which people engage with digital technologies for commerce

of the extent to which people engage with digital technologies for commerce 
and services. This lags global averages despite high broadband access, social 
media penetration, and government investments in e-government portals. It 
illustrates the regionʼs digital paradox: connectivity and internet use that have 
not translated into economic benefits.
Uneven digital transformation limits the potential resilience and inclusive 
development for MENAAP countries. Informal and small firms remain invisible 
to formal lenders, unable to demonstrate creditworthiness without verifiable 
digital records. Women are 12 percentage points less likely than men to use 
digital payments, the largest gender gap in digital finance globally. In the regionʼs 
fragile and conflict-affected settings such as Afghanistan, Lebanon, Syria, and 
Yemen, the building blocks for a functioning digital ecosystem are absent or

Yemen, the building blocks for a functioning digital ecosystem are absent or 
severely degraded, compounding vulnerabilities for populations most in need of 
public services. This decreases service and business continuity, participation in 
digital commerce, and access to economic opportunities. 
Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) presents an opportunity to improve service 
delivery and economic growth in the region. DPI refers to shared foundations 
for digital transformation, namely digital ID and e-signatures, digital payments, 
and data-sharing frameworks that enable digital service delivery at scale. DPI 
is also a foundation for artificial intelligence (AI) and for structuring high-quality, 
interoperable government data for applications that support policy decisions and 
process automation.

This diagnostic assesses the state of DPI across 21 MENAAP countries, 
drawing on the framework of a 2025 World Bank DPI and Development 
White Paper. It evaluates the following interconnected DPI elements: digital ID 
and e-signatures, digital payments (proxied by the presence and operational 
status of Fast Payment Systems), data sharing platforms, as well as the legal and 
institutional frameworks that enable and govern them. 3

Uneven Transformation Across a  
Diverse Region
The 21 MENAAP countries do not constitute a single digital transformation 
story, but rather three distinct tiers. The tiers reflect meaningful differences in 
DPI maturity, institutional capacity, and nature of reforms required.

Council (GCC)—are at the frontier. These countries have near-universal 
internet penetration, mature digital ID systems, operational real-time payment

of deepening. Persistent gender gaps signal that reach and equity have not 
kept pace with system sophistication. Structured regional cooperation on

Two related challenges define the regionʼs DPI landscape. Both challenges 
must be addressed on their own terms:
In more advanced economies, the gap lies between what has been built and 
what is used—a question of integration, adoption, inclusion, and governance. 
In LIC and FCS settings, significant infrastructure gaps remain: foundational 
systems are still missing or non-functional, and building them is prerequisite for 
everything else.

blocks are in place, they rarely work together.  Key missing building blocks 
include undeployed or absent digital ID and FPS, Certificate Authorities, and 
data-sharing platforms; but even where these exist, digital ID systems are often 
not linked to payment rails, unified service portals sit atop fragmented back-end

On e-signatures, all 21 countries have enacted laws granting legal 
equivalence to electronic signatures, but many remain unused in practice.  
Several lack the implementing regulations and Certificate Authorities required to 
verify the identity of signers and issue trusted digital certificates, ensuring that

Several lack the implementing regulations and Certificate Authorities required to 
verify the identity of signers and issue trusted digital certificates, ensuring that 
an electronic signature is trustworthy. More than half of the regionʼs countries still 
require “wet” signatures for high-value transactions, real estate, wills, and judicial 
proceedings, narrowing the practical scope of digital contracting.
On payments, the picture is also mixed. Twelve of 21 countries have FPS, but 
nine have yet to deploy one. This is a foundational gap that integration alone 
cannot bridge. Where FPS exists, utilization remains the more pressing challenge: 
government payments are frequently routed outside national infrastructure, 
nonbank payment service provider (PSP) access is limited, and the absence 
of open application programming interfaces (API) constrains the ecosystem 
participation that would make payment DPIs function as genuine public goods.

On data sharing, the regional divide also tends to track country income 
levels. GCC countries have high-volume, mature platforms. Leading MICs have 
made progress. Most LICs and FCSs, with the exception of the West Bank and 
Gaza, lack operational infrastructure.
On legal enablers and governance, DPI functions are distributed across 
various ministries (ICT and digital economy, interior, and finance), as well 
as central banks and sometimes dedicated agencies.  Whole-of-government

Verifiable Credentials (VCs) and digital wallets are emerging as the next 
evolution of digital identity.  A VC is a digital document issued by a trusted 
authority (such as a government) that confirms specific information about a 
person—their identity, qualifications, or entitlement to a benefit, among other 
examples. VCs are tamper-evident and can be checked by a third party without

person—their identity, qualifications, or entitlement to a benefit, among other

needing to contact the original issuer each time. A digital wallet is an application, 
typically on a mobile phone, in which people store their credentials and choose 
what to share, with whom, and when. This shifts digital identity toward a model 
in which individuals hold their own credentials and decide what to disclose. 
Through selective sharing, a person can prove, for instance, that they are over 
age 18 or employed by a particular firm without revealing other personal details, 
reducing unnecessary data exposure.

a substitute for them.  Their reliability depends on trusted issuers, functional

• a foundational digital ID system capable of supporting trusted issuance; 
• a legal framework that recognizes digital credentials as equivalent to their 
physical counterparts; 
• alignment with international technical standards (such as W3C Verifiable 
Credentials and ISO/IEC 18013-5) to enable interoperability across systems

transactions within DPI ecosystems, shaping how individuals, businesses, and 
governments authenticate transactions and execute legally binding actions in

Data sharing as DPI refers to the technical and governance infrastructure

support services at societal scale.  Data sharing allows verified authorized
